facts.raw_span: A woman in her 60s with a history of hypertension
sudden-onset chest pain
no history of any acute febrile illness
no family history of sudden cardiac death
tachycardic with a pulse of 120 beats/min
blood pressure was normal
White blood cell count: 14,300/µL
Serum calcium: within normal limits
High-sensitivity troponin I: 1.15 ng/mL
Brain-type natriuretic peptide: 1060.30 pg/mL
Initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia, PR-segment elevation in lead aVR, PR-segment depression in leads I, II, III, aVF, and V4 to V6
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: revealed an enhanced left-adrenal heterogeneous mass measuring 4.1 × 3.4 cm
A woman in her 60s with a history of hypertension

High-sensitivity troponin I: 1.15 ng/mL
Brain-type natriuretic peptide: 1060.30 pg/mL
Initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia, PR-segment elevation in lead aVR, PR-segment depression in leads I, II, III, aVF, and V4 to V6
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: revealed an enhanced left-adrenal heterogeneous mass measuring 4.1 × 3.4 cm

concepts.why: The presence of an enhanced left-adrenal heterogeneous mass on the abdominal CT suggests a pheochromocytoma, which is a type of adrenal gland tumor.

The patient's presentation with sudden-onset chest pain, elevated troponin and brain-type natriuretic peptide levels, and the ECG findings are consistent with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, which is further supported by the left ventriculography showing systolic apical ballooning.
The patient's history of hypertension and the presence of tachycardia suggest a possible hypertensive crisis, although the blood pressure is currently normal.

The elevated troponin and brain-type natriuretic peptide levels suggest myocardial damage, which could be due to a myocardial infarction, although the coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries.

The presence of an adrenal mass and the patient's cardiac symptoms suggest a possible catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy, which could be due to excessive catecholamine production by the adrenal tumor.
